title: Chapter 7: Modern JavaScript and V8 Engine Mechanics

blocks.text: JavaScript has evolved from a simple browser scripting utility into one of the world's most widely deployed computing runtimes. Through Google's **V8 engine**, JavaScript powers enterprise servers via Node.js and full-featured cross-platform desktop applications via Electron. For an engineer building full-stack web and desktop software, understanding the JavaScript single-threaded event loop and asynchronous concurrency model is mandatory.
The V8 Engine and Single-Threaded Execution Model

JavaScript executes inside an engine such as Google V8 (written in C++). Unlike multi-threaded languages like C++ or Java where operating system threads execute code concurrently, JavaScript operates on a **single main execution thread** with a single Call Stack.

blocks.text: When asynchronous operations complete (such as network I/O or timers), their callback functions are scheduled into queues:

blocks.title: Key Highlights
lines: • **Macrotask Queue**: Houses timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`) and filesystem/network callbacks.

blocks.text:
**The Event Loop Draining Invariant:**
The Event Loop continuously checks if the Call Stack is empty. When empty:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item It **drains the entire Microtask Queue completely** until empty.
 \item Only after every microtask has executed does it pick **exactly one Macrotask** from the Macrotask Queue and push it to the Call Stack.
\end{enumerate}
This invariant explains why a resolved Promise callback will always execute **before** a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` timer callback!

blocks.text:
**Question**: *“If JavaScript is single-threaded, how does it handle thousands of concurrent network connections in Node.js without blocking?”*
**Defense**: *“JavaScript's execution engine is single-threaded, but the underlying runtime (Node.js) is powered by **Libuv**, a C library that leverages kernel-level asynchronous I/O multiplexing: `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS, and `IOCP` on Windows. When an I/O request is made, the operating system kernel notifies the runtime upon packet arrival. Only the lightweight completion callback executes on the JavaScript thread, allowing a single thread to handle tens of thousands of idle connections without thread switching overhead.”*

**Pitfall: Unhandled Promise Rejections & Floating Promises:**
In modern Node.js, failing to catch a rejected Promise will trigger an `UnhandledPromiseRejection` event and terminate the entire Node process. Never invoke an `async` function without either an `await` inside a `try...catch` block or attaching a `.catch()` handler to the resulting Promise.
